question: What does a version control system record, and what can it restore?
expected_answer: It records changes to files over time, including who changed what, and can restore an earlier version.

gold.evidence:
A version control system (VCS) is software that records changes to files over time, so
you can see who changed what and bring back any earlier version.

question: Why can another developer's copy help recover a project when one computer is lost in a distributed VCS?
expected_answer: Every developer has a complete copy of the project and its whole history, so another copy can be used for recovery.

gold.evidence:
3. Distributed VCS. Every developer has a complete copy of the project and its whole
history on their own computer. Examples: Git and Mercurial. Like every student owning
a full photocopy of the book: if one copy is lost, any other copy can replace it.

question: In Unit 1, how should a student set their Git author name on a shared lab PC so the next student's commits do not use that name?
expected_answer: Set the name without --global inside the student's own project folder, so it applies to that repository.

gold.evidence:
On a shared lab PC, set your name without              --global     inside your own project
   folder, so the next student's commits are not labelled with your name.

question: Which hidden folder does git init create, and what does that folder contain?
expected_answer: It creates .git, which contains the repository's history, branches and settings.

gold.evidence:
git init     creates one hidden folder,       .git   . That folder is the repository: all history,
branches and settings live inside it.

question: A developer fixes a bug and starts a feature during the same hour. How does the staging area help keep their commits separate?
expected_answer: The staging area lets the developer select changes for each snapshot and commit the bug fix and feature as two separate commits.

gold.evidence:
Why have a staging area at all? Because real work is messy. You may fix a bug and
start a new feature in the same hour. Staging lets you commit them as two clean,
separate commits.

question: Why does downloading a GitHub ZIP not provide the same repository capabilities as git clone?
expected_answer: The ZIP has only the files, without history or a GitHub connection, so it cannot be used to push or pull. A clone includes the whole history and configures origin.

gold.evidence:
git clone      downloads every file and the whole history, and sets up               origin     for you.
That's why you don't run        git init     or  git remote add        after cloning.

   ⚠Clone ≠ Download ZIP

   GitHub's Download ZIP button gives you only the files: no history and no
   connection to GitHub. You can't push or pull from it.

question: A teammate pushed first and Git rejects my push. According to the book, what should I do instead of forcing the push?
expected_answer: Run git pull, then git push again; do not force the push.

gold.evidence:
If a teammate pushed before you, Git refuses your push. Never panic and never
   force it: run  git pull    , then   git push     again.

question: Does git branch feature-menu also switch the working branch to feature-menu?
expected_answer: No. It creates a branch at the current commit but does not switch to it.

gold.evidence:
git branch <name>         creates a branch at your current commit, but it does not
   switch to it.

question: After deciding the correct contents of a conflicted file, what must I remove and which two Git steps finish the merge?
expected_answer: Remove all three conflict marker lines, stage the resolved file with git add, and finish with git commit.

gold.evidence:

question: In Unit 3, can I delete the branch I am currently standing on, and what must I do first?
expected_answer: No. Switch away from the current branch before deleting it.

gold.evidence: You can't delete the branch you are standing on; switch away first.

question: By default, will git stash save brand-new files that have never been added to Git?
expected_answer: No. By default it saves changes to tracked files; brand-new files that were never added stay where they are.

gold.evidence:
By default,    git stash      saves changes to tracked files. Brand-new files you
   never added stay where they are.

question: Why can plain git diff show nothing immediately after git add moves my change to the staging area?
expected_answer: The change has moved to the staging area, so there is no unstaged change for plain git diff to show.

gold.evidence:
Notice that after    git add    , plain  git diff     shows nothing: the change moved to the
staging area.

question: A broken commit has already been pushed and teammates have pulled it. Which undo command preserves the shared history, and how?
expected_answer: Use git revert. It adds a new commit that reverses the old change instead of rewriting the shared history.

gold.evidence:
Not pushed yet?       reset     is fine: you're only rewriting your own history. Already
   pushed? Use       revert    . It adds a new commit and never rewrites history your
   team already has.

git revert <commit>         creates a new commit that does the opposite of the old one.
The history stays honest: anyone can see the mistake and its fix. Without              --no-edit    ,
Git opens the editor with a ready-made message.

question: In Unit 4, are tags pushed automatically, and which command publishes all local tags?
expected_answer: No. Push all tags explicitly with git push origin --tags.

gold.evidence:
Tags are not pushed
automatically: use      git push origin v1.1        , or  git push origin --tags          for all of
them.
